title: Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
output:
Stand directly in front of Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, about two metres back, with the barmaid at eye level. From here you can see her face, the long gold frame of the mirror behind her, and the reflected crowd all at once. Then take a few steps to the right and look at the man on the far right edge. Moving shifts how the reflection reads, and that is the key to the whole picture.

The painting is oil on canvas, about four and a quarter feet wide, and its central trick is a mirror running the full length of the picture. In front of that mirror stands a young woman named Suzon, a real barmaid at the Folies-Bergère, the Paris music hall and nightclub where this scene is set. Manet did not paint her on location. He posed her in his studio, which is why her face has the fixed, almost sculpted calm of someone holding still for a long sitting.

Look at the reflection. Her back appears at the far right, bent toward a man in a top hat as if deep in conversation. Yet the woman facing you stands upright at the centre, withdrawn and distant. The two views do not match, and critics accused Manet of botching his perspective from the first reviews. In 2000, the art historian Malcolm Park built a physical reconstruction of the scene and showed the geometry holds. The man is not standing in front of her at all. He stands to the left, outside the painter's field of vision, and looks away. The conversation we assume is an optical trick. A preliminary study placed her off to the right, and Manet moved her to the centre of the canvas while leaving her reflection where it was. That choice costs the viewer certainty. You cannot say where you are standing.

The still life on the marble counter carries meaning too. The bowl of oranges, according to the art historian Larry Ligo, is a code Manet habitually used to mark a woman as a prostitute. The scholar T. J. Clark argues she is shown as both a salesperson and a commodity, something to be bought along with a drink. Now look to the upper left corner, where a pair of small green feet dangle. They belong to a trapeze artist performing above the crowd, and Manet gives them no more space than a footnote. The mirror also recalls Las Meninas, the court painting by Diego Velázquez, an artist Manet admired. Velázquez used a mirror to complicate who is watching whom, and the philosopher Michel Foucault's discussion of that painting in The Order of Things in 1966 reopened the comparison for modern readers.

This was Manet's last major work. He painted it in 1882 and showed it at the Paris Salon that year, the official annual exhibition. He died in 1883, so the picture belongs to the final months of a life spent pushing realism, the commitment to showing contemporary Paris as it really looked. It originally belonged to his close friend, the composer Emmanuel Chabrier, and hung over his piano.

At the Courtauld, the painting came with Samuel Courtauld's collection, which also included a version of the Déjeuner sur l'Herbe and a group of eight major works by Cézanne. It now hangs in the Great Room alongside Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces.

Step back once more to the barmaid's face. The crowd glitters behind her, and she stays still. Her gaze goes nowhere, and the painting never says what she is thinking.

title: Van Gogh’s iconic Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
output:
Stand a few steps back from Van Gogh's iconic Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear, centered in front of it, so that his face sits at your eye level. From here you can read the whole stack of the picture at once: the man, the easel behind him, and the print pinned beside it. Step closer afterward, and the surface breaks into thick ridges of paint.

Van Gogh shows himself in a blue cap trimmed with black fur and a green overcoat. A white bandage wraps over his ear and runs under his chin. His eyes look out at you, steady and tired. Behind him on the left is a canvas on an easel, with a few marks on it that tell you nothing. On the right hangs a Japanese woodblock print, Geishas in a Landscape, by Satō Torakiyo, made in the 1870s. At the top is an open window.

Look at how the paint was applied. Van Gogh used impasto, a technique where paint is laid on thickly so that the marks of the brush or palette knife stay visible. Here it gives the coat and cap a heavy, almost sculpted surface and puts energy into every edge. He had learned to admire this approach in the paintings of Adolphe Monticelli, a French painter whose thick, jewel-like surfaces Van Gogh praised in a letter to his brother Theo in 1888.

The cap has a story too. It was bought to hold the heavy bandage in place and to keep out the winter cold, so it records the practical misery of January 1889. Van Gogh told Theo in a letter dated 17 January that he had made a new self-portrait, and this is believed to be it.

The bandage is on the wrong side. Van Gogh sliced off his left ear, but he painted himself from a mirror, which reverses everything, so the bandage appears over his right ear. He had moved from Paris to Arles, in the south of France, to found a community of supportive artists he called the Studio of the South. He rented four rooms in the Yellow House and invited Paul Gauguin to join him. On the evening of 23 December 1888, Gauguin threatened to leave, and Van Gogh approached him with a razor. That night he cut off his ear and brought it to a woman in Arles named Rachel. She was distressed, and the police were called. The dream of a shared studio ended there.

The print behind him matters because Van Gogh collected Japanese woodblock prints, hundreds of them over his life. He loved their bold colour and flattened space, and he used those qualities to modernise his own style. Here the print sits beside his bandaged head as an equal presence, a reminder of the kind of art he was trying to build a life around.

The picture does not ask for pity. His gaze is level, the colours are calm greens and blues set against a hard orange-red behind him, and the injury is stated plainly as one more fact among the cap, the easel, and the print.

The painting came to the Courtauld through Samuel Courtauld, who bought it in 1928.

It is one of the best-known works in a collection famous for its Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings, and it hangs among works by Manet and Cézanne that explore the same moment when painters broke from tradition.

Before it reached London, it belonged to Julien Tanguy, the Paris colour merchant who had posed twice for Van Gogh in 1887. He still had it when Van Gogh died.

title: Georges Seurat
output:
Stand directly in front of Georges Seurat's Young Woman Powdering Herself, about two metres back, and look at the top left corner first. From this distance the whole surface holds together as a seated woman at her dressing table, and the small vase of flowers up in that corner, which looks like an afterthought, is what you came to see.

The painting shows a young woman at her toilette, bare to the waist, leaning toward a mirror with a powder puff in her raised hand. She is Madeleine Knobloch, Seurat's mistress, and the mother of his two sons. That makes this an intimate subject, a private moment in a private room, painted by the man who knew her best.

The surface is built from small dots of pure colour, set side by side in varying concentrations rather than mixed on a palette. The theory behind this, which Seurat developed with Paul Signac and which became known as pointillism, holds that the eye blends adjacent dots into a single tone at a distance. Seurat believed this gave a brighter, more luminous result than muddied pigment. You can see it at work in the wall behind her, where light and shadow are modulated entirely by the changing density of those dots. Step close and the wall breaks into a field of separate flecks. Step back and it becomes soft, even light.

Now return to that corner. A scan made by the Italian Institute of Optics revealed that the vase of flowers was not the original design. Underneath, the image was a reflection of Seurat himself at work, painted into the mirror. If so, it would have been the only self-portrait he ever made. He covered it over, and the flowers took its place. What he gave up was the one record of his own face.

Seurat was in his late twenties, living in Paris, and at this point he had completed his great public canvases, the big outdoor scenes of modern leisure. This painting belongs to the closing years of that work, dated to about 1888 to 1890. He would die in 1891, aged thirty-one. So this is a late picture from a very short career, and its subject is domestic and hidden from view, quite unlike the crowds he had painted before.

The painting also hints at why he removed himself. A figure peering out of the mirror would have turned a quiet portrait of Madeleine into a picture about the watcher. Painted over, the room belongs to her alone, and he is present only as the unseen eye behind the dots.

It hangs here among the Courtauld's Impressionist and Post-Impressionist works, alongside Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère and Cézanne, and it came to the gallery through Samuel Courtauld's collection.

Look at the flowers once more. Beneath them is the artist's own reflection, still there under the paint.

title: The Death of Caesar
output:
I have to flag a problem before the script itself. The source material places "The Death of Caesar" by Vincenzo Camuccini in the National Museum of Capodimonte in Naples. It has been there since 1864, and nothing in the sources connects it to the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore. The Walters material describes other works entirely. I have therefore written the stop around the painting and its maker as documented, and I have not claimed that the Walters owns it. If the Walters does hold a version, a copy, or a loan, please confirm that and I will add the venue connection and the physical details, which the sources do not give.

**Audio description: The Death of Caesar, Vincenzo Camuccini, 1806**

**Orientation**

Stand a few paces back from The Death of Caesar and let your eye settle on the center of the canvas, where Caesar is going down. From here you can take in the whole ring of senators at once. Close up, you read individual faces. From a distance, you see what the painter built: a crowd arranged like a stage, every figure turned toward one falling man.

**The Work**

The Death of Caesar shows the assassination of Julius Caesar, the Roman general and dictator, stabbed by a group of senators in 44 BC. Camuccini painted it in 1806, and it is an oil painting in the Neoclassical manner. That means he composed it the way an ancient relief sculpture would be composed, with the figures arranged across the front of the picture in clear, balanced groups rather than in swirling depth.

The key fact about how it was made is that it was made twice. Camuccini completed a cartoon, a full-size preparatory drawing, in 1793. Roman art critics received it favorably. But when he painted a first version in 1796, it was less well received. So he destroyed it and started again from scratch. The painting you see is the second attempt, finished in 1806. Ten years separate the cartoon from the final canvas, and one entire painting was sacrificed along the way. That severity is part of the picture's character: nothing here is casual.

Its fate was also uncertain. It was commissioned in 1793 by Frederick Hervey, the 4th Earl of Bristol, an English aristocrat and collector. But the Earl died in 1803, and his heirs refused to pay. Camuccini was left with a finished masterpiece and no buyer. In 1807 he sold it to Joachim Murat, the French marshal who ruled Naples under Napoleon. After Murat's fall it passed to Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies, who hung it in the royal palace in Naples, and in 1864 it moved to its present home in the National Museum of Capodimonte.

**The Artist**

Vincenzo Camuccini was working in Rome, the center of Neoclassicism, the movement that turned to ancient Greece and Rome for its subjects and its discipline. By 1793 he was already trusted by the Earl of Bristol, for whom he had made a copy of Raphael's Deposition, a famous Renaissance painting of Christ being lowered from the cross. Copying Raphael was training in order and clarity, and you can feel it here. The Caesar commission was his chance to prove he could do more than copy a master. He could build a great history painting of his own, and he was willing to destroy a canvas that fell short of that.

**The Emotional Reading**

The controlled arrangement is what makes the scene unsettling. The violence is staged with the calm of a classical frieze, so the stillness around Caesar feels colder than chaos would. Knowing the painter burned his own first attempt, you sense a man unwilling to settle for anything less than exactness.

title: The Laughing Cavalier
output:
Stand directly in front of The Laughing Cavalier, close enough to see the surface, then step slightly to one side and back again. His eyes seem to follow you. That effect comes from his gaze aimed straight out at the painter's position, so it lands on you wherever you stand. From close range, look at his raised right sleeve, which is where the picture rewards you most.

The painting is by Frans Hals, dated 1624. It measures about 83 by 67 centimetres, smaller than most people expect. The inscription at top right reads "aetatis suae 26, anno 1624," Latin for "aged 26, in the year 1624." So the man was born in 1597 or 1598. No one knows who he was. One art historian, Pieter Biesboer, has suggested he may be Tieleman Roosterman, a Dutch cloth merchant, who sat for Hals on another occasion. He could just as easily have been a wealthy civilian as a soldier.

The title is a Victorian invention. When the painting first appeared in London, at the Bethnal Green Museum in 1872, the catalogue called it simply "A Cavalier." By 1888 it had become the "Laughing Cavalier," and prints of it spread across Britain. But he is not laughing. He has an enigmatic smile, and the upturned tips of his moustache exaggerate it.

Now look at the sleeve. The costume is silk, very expensive, and it looks laboured, but close inspection shows long, quick brushstrokes. Hals painted with speed, and that choice matters here: the sitter seems caught mid-turn rather than posed. The turning pose and low viewpoint put the sleeve and lace cuff right in front of you.

The embroidery on that sleeve is a code. Bees, arrows, flaming cornucopiae, which are overflowing horns of plenty set alight, lovers' knots and tongues of fire stand for the pleasures and pains of love. An obelisk or pyramid signifies strength. Mercury's winged cap and his caduceus, the staff entwined with snakes, signify fortune. He is wearing his hopes on his arm.

Frans Hals was a Dutch Golden Age portraitist working in Haarlem. In 1624 he was painting sitters with an unusual freedom. Commissioned portraits of adults rarely showed smiles until the late eighteenth century, though smiling appears in tronies, which are character studies of costumed types, and in everyday-life scenes. Hals broke the rule, often giving sitters broader smiles and looser poses than this one. The source here says nothing more about his circumstances that year, so the painting itself is the evidence of his ambition: to make a stiff genre feel alive.

That ambition shows. Art historian Seymour Slive called it "one of the most brilliant of all Baroque portraits." The man holds your gaze, and the glint at the corner of his mouth holds it longer.

The Marquess of Hertford bought it at a Paris auction in 1865, outbidding Baron James de Rothschild at more than six times the estimate. Its fame in England helped raise Hals's reputation there.

He is twenty-six, he has spent a fortune on his clothes, and he has stitched his private hopes into a sleeve.

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
output:
Stand a few steps back from the canvas, near the centre of the gallery, so that the whole picture sits in your field of view. From here you can take in the ring of dancers and the sky above them in a single glance. Then let your eye travel upward from the dancers to the band of sunrise behind them. That vertical reading is the key to this painting.

A Dance to the Music of Time shows four figures holding hands in a circle, turning in rhythm. At the right sits Time, a winged, naked, grey-bearded old man, playing a lyre. Above and behind, the sky holds a second procession. Aurora, goddess of the dawn, goes ahead of the chariot of Apollo, the sun god, with the Hours moving alongside him. Apollo holds a ring that stands for the Zodiac, the band of constellations the sun appears to cross over a year. The earthly dance and the heavenly procession are one clock in two registers, the dancers turning below as the sun climbs above.

Who the dancers are has never been settled. According to the seventeenth-century biographer Gian Pietro Bellori, the patron, Giulio Rospigliosi, dictated the subject. He was a cultivated writer with a taste for allegory, and he later became Pope Clement IX. In Bellori's account the four are Poverty, Labour, Riches, and Pleasure or Luxury, a cycle in which Pleasure leads back to Poverty again. Poussin's friend and biographer André Félibien told it the same way, except that he named the last figure Pleasure where Bellori said Luxury. Read as the Four Seasons, Poverty is Autumn and Labour is Winter. The figure at the back, seen mostly from behind, is now generally accepted as male, which is unusual for a group of Seasons, and the museum describes him as Bacchus, god of wine. The story behind that reading is that mortals and the Seasons complained of life's miseries, and Jupiter answered by giving the world Bacchus and his wine as compensation.

Not everyone accepts that this was the original plan. The scholar Malcolm Bull traces the imagery to the late Greek poet Nonnus, as echoed in a French hymn to autumn by Pierre de Ronsard. In that source, Spring wears roses in her hair, Autumn has olive branches on her brow, Winter has bound hair and a shadowed face, and Summer wears white with ears of corn braided into her hair. Bull suggests Rospigliosi invented the Poverty-and-Riches interpretation during or after the painting's completion. Another scholar, Ingamells, thinks Poussin was not unduly concerned with identifying each figure precisely. Notice the stone herma, a pillar topped with a head, at the left. Its two faces, one young and one old, show Bacchus in his double aspect.

Look closely at the surface and you will find the traces of Poussin changing his mind. These are called pentimenti, the visible remnants of earlier decisions. Between Winter and Time on the right, he painted out a second, larger tree. The painting is in generally good condition, but a large L-shaped tear runs right through the central group of dancers. It was repaired and retouched, so the wound is mended but part of that area is no longer purely Poussin's hand.

Nicolas Poussin was a French painter who made his career in Rome. This canvas dates from around 1634 to 1636, when he was working there on commissions from learned patrons who wanted paintings that rewarded close reading. This was a commission from an intellectual, built on a program supplied by the patron, and Poussin turned it into a picture where the argument is carried by gesture and rhythm. The circle has no leader and no end. Each dancer is joined to the next, and the chain pulls toward the viewer while the musician at the edge keeps time.

The title is a later arrival. It first appears in a Wallace Collection catalogue of 1913. Earlier, the picture went by names referring to the Four Seasons, and an 1845 sale called it The Dance of the Seasons, or the Image of Human Life. The novelist Anthony Powell borrowed the phrase for his twelve-novel cycle, and in its opening pages his narrator, Nicholas Jenkins, sees the picture in a fire and thinks of mortality, of people moving hand in hand in intricate measure.

The dancers do not look at each other or at Time. They face outward, hands locked, stepping to a tune they cannot stop, while the sun behind them is already rising.

title: Madame de Pompadour
output:
Stand a few steps back from Madame de Pompadour, near the centre of the canvas, so you take in the whole figure at once. From there the painting reads as a single sweep of colour and fabric, and you can see how the skirt, the sitter, and the setting are arranged to move your eye from the hem upward to her face.

This is an oil painting on canvas, made in 1759 by the French Rococo painter François Boucher. Rococo is the playful, ornamental style that flourished in eighteenth-century France, favouring soft colour, curving lines, and scenes of leisure over the weight of earlier court art. It was the last of seven portraits Boucher painted of Madame de Pompadour. That number matters. He returned to the same sitter again and again, which means this canvas is the end of a long visual conversation between painter and subject, not a single commission.

The sitter was one of the most powerful women in France, the official mistress of King Louis XV, a role that gave her real influence at court as well as social standing. A portrait of her was never only a likeness. It was a statement of status, taste, and presence, meant to be seen by the court.

Boucher's handling of paint is the clue to how he achieves that. The Rococo habit of rendering fabric as a landscape of its own is on full display here: surfaces of silk and ribbon are built from small, light touches that catch the eye before the face does. The effect is deliberate. The viewer is invited to read wealth and refinement in the materials first, and the woman second.

The painting was first shown at the Château de Versailles, the royal palace outside Paris where the court lived, so its earliest audience was the very society that Pompadour moved within. It later passed to her brother, a fact that follows the portrait out of the palace and into private family hands.

Boucher was among the leading painters of the French court at this point in his career. By 1759 he had spent years painting this one woman, and this canvas closes that series. I have no documented account of his state of mind or the circumstances of this final sitting, so what the painting tells us is limited to what is on the canvas itself.

Look at how much of the picture is given over to dress and surface, and how the sitter's face sits within it rather than dominating it. That balance suggests a woman presented as inseparable from the world of luxury around her, composed and fully aware of being looked at.

The Wallace Collection holds a great deal of eighteenth-century French art, and this portrait belongs among it as a record of the court style that Boucher helped define.

title: Officer and Laughing Girl
output:
Stand a few steps back from Officer and Laughing Girl, directly in front of the canvas and at the height of the woman's face. From here the whole small picture holds together: the soldier's dark bulk in the near foreground, the girl's lit face across the table, and the big map on the back wall. Move in close afterward, and you will see how little paint it takes to make her smile.

The painting is oil on canvas, about fifty by forty-six centimeters, so it is smaller than most people expect. Look first at the soldier. He is cut almost to a silhouette, a mass of red coat and a wide-brimmed hat, and he sits right at the front of the picture, bigger than the woman across from him. Painters call this device repoussoir, a French word for an object placed in the foreground to push the rest of the scene backward and deepen the space. Vermeer probably learned it from followers of Caravaggio, the Italian master of theatrical shadow. His hat is beaver felt, and the pelts for such hats came from the New World, probably from New Netherland, the Dutch colony in what is now the eastern United States. Light enters from an open window at the left, as it does in so many of Vermeer's rooms, and it falls softly on the girl's face while the officer stays in shadow.

Now look at the girl herself. She wears a yellow bodice with braiding, an everyday garment called a schort, and a blue apron mostly lost in the shadow of the table. Blue aprons were common because they hid stains. Scholars read this as a sign that the officer has dropped in on her during her morning chores. She holds a wine glass, the kind used for white wine, and wine cost more than beer in this period, so the glass hints at some means.

X-rays reveal what Vermeer changed. He first planned to paint her with a large white collar that would have covered much of the yellow dress. He also later extended her cap to hide all of her hair. Both changes strip away competing detail and send your eye straight to her face and expression. The face is where the painting puts its weight.

Behind them hangs a large map of Holland and West Friesland, published by Willem Blaeu and Balthasar Florisz van Berckenrode in 1621. It is mounted on linen and wooden rods, and Vermeer rendered it so precisely that it can be identified. He evidently owned a copy, because it appears in three of his paintings. The map ties this quiet room to Dutch commerce and exploration, the same trade that brought the beaver pelt to the officer's hat. Scholars think a painting by Gerard van Honthorst inspired the composition, and some believe Vermeer used a camera obscura, an early optical device that projects a scene onto a surface, to set up the perspective. Nobody agrees on what is happening between the two figures. Many see an honorable courtship, while others read her open hand and smile as a discreet willingness to go further.

Vermeer painted this around 1657, when he was in his mid-twenties, in Delft. The woman resembles his wife, Catharina Bolnes, who is believed to have posed for many of his paintings. Here he assembles for the first time many of the ingredients he would keep returning to: a woman in yellow, a window on the left, a map on the wall, a table that holds the figures in place.

What you notice is the stillness. The officer leans in and the girl laughs, yet the painting freezes the instant before anything is decided.

The Frick owns three Vermeers, and this one hangs alongside Girl Interrupted at Her Music and Mistress and Maid. This painting has also prompted new work from the contemporary artist Kent Monkman, who has taken it as a starting point to examine how paintings of its era depicted global trade and colonization.

title: Portrait of Sir Thomas More
output:
Stand a few feet back from Portrait of Sir Thomas More and look at the sitter's hands and chest rather than his face. From this distance the painting separates into its three working parts: the fur and velvet of the coat, the gold chain across the shoulders, and the small, plain objects that carry the real information. Closer in, those details dissolve into brushwork. Hold your ground and they stay legible.

Holbein painted this in 1527 on an oak panel. Oak was the standard support for northern European portraits of the period, and a panel gives a hard, smooth surface that lets a painter render fur, satin, and skin with almost no visible brushstroke. That is exactly what he does here. The coat is fur-lined, with black satin and red velvet. Notice how the red is the warmest thing in the picture, and how it frames a face that is otherwise cool, watchful, and still.

More is shown in three-quarter right half-profile, holding a book. Across his shoulders lies the Collar of Esses, a livery chain, meaning a badge of service to the crown, with a Tudor rose hanging from it. In Tudor England, wearing it announced fealty to the king and high office. At the time, More was a knighted figure who had risen to speak in Parliament.

Now look to the upper right, where a cord hangs tied in a loose Franciscan knot. This is a quiet sign of his spiritual convictions. Beside the glitter of the chain, it is easy to miss, and that placement is the point. The portrait holds two loyalties in the same frame, one to the king and one to faith. There is a third detail on his left index finger, a wedding ring set with a stone. The painting records a public official, a devout man, and a husband in a single glance.

Holbein was German, a painter and printmaker, and he had come to London in 1526. He arrived with an introduction from the Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus, the great scholar of the age, who recommended that Holbein befriend More. Humanists were scholars who revived classical learning and prized reasoned inquiry, and More was one of England's leading figures among them. This portrait grows out of that friendship and marks Holbein's entry into English society, where he would build his career painting the powerful.

The picture's afterlife shows how much it was valued. A closely related drawing in bodycolour, an opaque watercolour, is in the Royal Collection, though it was probably not a direct preparatory study. A copy in the National Portrait Gallery is thought to have been painted in Italy or Austria in the early seventeenth century. Holbein's other portrait of More, a large group picture of his family, is lost. Only drawings and copies survive, which makes this single panel the principal painted record of More's face by Holbein.

What stays with a viewer is the contrast between the richness of the clothes and the steadiness of the expression. The satin and velvet are lavish, yet the eyes do not perform for you. Knowing that the knotted cord and the ring sit just beside the chain of office, you begin to read the face as the place where those pulls meet.

Elsewhere in the building, the Frick's current Gainsborough exhibition shows how portraits shaped fashion in the eighteenth century. This panel shows an earlier version of the same idea, where cloth, chains, and rings were chosen to say who a person was.

title: Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville
output:
Stand directly in front of Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville, about six feet back and level with the sitter's face. From here the painting works as Ingres intended. Her gaze meets yours head-on, and the mirror behind her, which shows the back of her head and the line of her neck, falls into view. Step off to one side and you lose that confrontation.

Louise de Broglie was twenty-seven when Ingres finished this canvas in 1845. She stands fully frontal in a heavily folded satin dress, a cold grey-blue painted in the same hue as her eyes. Her hair is parted, with a crimson ribbon at the back. The palette is restrained: pale blue, grey, brown, gold and white. Look at her left hand. The index finger rests lightly against her mouth, a coy, half-thoughtful gesture, and it is the motif Ingres kept through every version of this portrait. Now follow her right arm. It is unnaturally long and sinuous, bending in a way no real arm would. Ingres chose elegance of line over anatomical accuracy, a habit critics had noted in his work since his Grande Odalisque of 1814.

Behind her is the mirror, a device Ingres first used in his 1814 portrait of Madame de Senonnes. The mirror lets him show the sitter from two angles at once. Beside it, a dresser holds writing materials, small pots, flowers, and a lavishly decorated oriental vase. The writing materials suit her. Louise was highly educated and later became an essayist and biographer, and she published historical romance novels based on the lives of Lord Byron, the English poet, Robert Emmett, the Irish rebel leader, and Margaret of Valois, a sixteenth-century French queen.

Ingres had tried this portrait once before. Two or three years earlier he made a black chalk sketch and started an oil version, but that canvas excluded the mirror and reversed the pose. The sittings were long and slow, and Louise found them wearisome. She complained that for nine days he had been painting on a single hand. Then she became pregnant with her third child and could no longer stand for him. The 1842 painting was abandoned, unfinished. So the work in front of you is a second attempt, begun after the first had stalled on the sitter's own exhaustion.

Ingres took this commission reluctantly. By 1845 his fame was at its height and portraits were in demand, but he considered them a distraction from history painting, the grand mythological and classical scenes he believed were the true calling of an artist. History painting paid far worse. He committed to only two portraits at the time, this one and the Baronne de Rothschild. Today it is for portraits like these that he is best known.

He was not satisfied. He wrote that Louise's family, her friends, and above all her father, the duc de Broglie, were delighted. The statesman Adolphe Thiers visited and told her, "M. Ingres must be in love with you to have painted you that way." Ingres replied that none of this made him proud, and that he had not conveyed all the graces of his charming model. The painting is signed and dated at the lower left.

In 1846 it was shown at the Bonne-Nouvelle exhibition beside the Grande Odalisque and the Odalisque with Slave. The poet Charles Baudelaire praised all three for their voluptuousness and called Ingres the quintessential painter of women. The intensity of the sitter's look has often been compared to that of his later portrait of Madame Moitessier.

Notice how little the satin moves. It falls in stiff, sculptural folds, and her gaze is demure yet direct. The cool blue of the dress and the cool blue of her eyes are the same colour, and that match is what holds her so still.

The painting hangs at the Frick, a museum known for its portraiture, which this spring is giving a whole exhibition to Thomas Gainsborough, the English painter whose portraits were shaped by fashion. Ingres paints a different world, but he too treats clothing as part of the sitter's presence. Here the dress is the same blue as her eyes.
